comment: Same Commission series and same total of 23, but 14 then 13 with EU Member States, and the 2021 report says there were no changes in this area. No definition or date explains it.

The list is a heading plus rows and states no total. It separates 22 concluded agreements from 6 conventions taken over from the former SFRY, so any count depends on what is included. 23 matches neither subtotal, and the source does not explain how 23 was reached.

23 in place against 22 signed, in the same period, with 13 EU agreements in both and no agreement recorded as ending. Agreements in place cannot exceed agreements signed. The Commission itself gives 22 (13) in 2024 (MKD-EU-2024-001-0064).

Same law, about one year apart: no distinction between EU citizens and other foreigners, against quotas that do not apply to EU citizens. The Commission assessment in the same screening report still asks the country to exclude EU citizens from the annual quotas.

Scope explains the gap. The nine match the Member States with EHIC agreements in the screening report (MKD-EU-2025-003, pages 29 and 103). The five added are all named there as having social care agreements that do not include EHIC. The wording of both items blurs this, so the figures need careful labelling.

Different bases are likely. The 2021 report counts work permits for foreign workers. The screening report gives a share of single work and residence permits, 'such cases'. Neither states its denominator fully, so the explanation is probable and not proven.

Different scope. The strategy's 'vacuum' follows from having no new ICT strategy since 2017, while the Commission rates the institutional set-up. The Commission's same paragraph also asks for attention to capacity. The dates differ by eight months.

Different level. The audit finds one specific gap between the ministry and the innovation fund on AI programmes. The Commission gives a general rating of the digital policy set-up. A sector gap can coexist with a general positive rating.

Different objects. ITU describes a ministers' council monitoring sectoral ICT and eGovernment projects. The audit's absent body concerns systems shared by several institutions, and elsewhere it says a council for interoperability was never formed. A tension remains on how far coordination worked in practice.

Different functions. The strategy says no institution is competent for implementation or inspection. The Commission says the ministry leads on digitalisation projects, and in the same sentence says modernisation lacks clear ownership. The two descriptions are largely compatible.

Both 2025 and about the same legislation: aligned with European standards, especially the GDPR, against adoption of legislation to fully align with the GDPR still pending. The audit states no limit on its claim. The gap is partly one of degree.

North Macedonia says it is aligned on the use of digital tools and processes. The Commission asks for further alignment in its 2023, 2024 and 2025 reports, and in the same screening report asks for alignment with Directive (EU) 2019/1151. The Commission does also record a high level of alignment on disclosure.

Different function and date. The 2024 audit describes the portal mailbox for delivering documents. The 2025 strategy plans a mailbox that gives institutions proof of the day of receipt, because delivery dates cannot currently be established.

The status agrees: not adopted. The audit quotes the title of one draft, version 1.1 published in June 2021, while the Commission uses a looser name. A later draft may have had another period. No source shows this, and the difference has no analytical effect.

Different counts and dates. The Commission counts services by administrative bodies accessible on the portal in April 2022. ITU counts single sign-on e-services from an earlier snapshot. The audit series moves from 50 to 212 between August 2021 and May 2022, so the count was changing fast.

Different definition and probably date. 203 allow e-application by September 2022. 95 is a strategy baseline for 2022 with no month, and a footnote on page 37 of the strategy ties the number of services to the fourth level of sophistication. The audit series gives 212 in May 2022.

Definitions differ but are not fully stated. The strategy counts e-services at the fourth level of sophistication, and its footnote is an unfinished note on that level. 'Fully automated' is undefined. The 230 sits close to the audit series (224 to 234), while the 95 appears to be an earlier baseline.

Counting definitions probably differ. The audit separates its 234 e-services from 162 services on external portals reached through redirects, and 277 reached through the portal. The Commission's 392 'digital services' is undefined. Its own report also gives 230 and 238, so its counting is inconsistent.

Different measures. The Commission's 5% has no stated source or year. The 22% is a Balkan Barometer opinion survey in which citizens report their own use. Survey self-reporting and a population usage figure are not the same indicator.

Different indicators. The 36% is the overall maturity score (EU27+ biennial average). The strategy's own formula (page 147) defines 47.4% as the mean of user centricity and key enablers only. The name 'benchmark' hides the difference.

Same Reform Agenda target of a 50% increase, published the same day in October 2024: a baseline of 264 against a current figure of 392. Being the base of one target, they should measure the same thing, and neither states a different definition. The baseline for a payment-linked step is therefore unclear.

Same portal in the same two months: 264 e-services against 124 services where applications can be submitted electronically. No narrower definition is stated. The 124 is also below the audit's 234 e-services of November 2023, so growth does not explain it.

Definition probably explains it. 124 are services where applications can be submitted electronically, while 392 is a wider and undefined 'digital services' count whose sentence repeats the 2023 report. The audit's categories show that such wider counts exist. Probable, not proven.

Same author, same portal, three months apart, and almost the same description: services available to citizens and businesses online. The number halves between June and September 2024 with no stated change of definition. Commission counts of this indicator are not reliable as a series.

Both about the same period. The Commission says most administrative services are offered online and offline. The audit's portal data show 1,120 services only in person, against 162 and 277 reachable online, or about 72% in person. Its own next sentences say the most common services are not online.

North Macedonia says the platform allows access to people with disabilities. The audit finds that visually impaired people cannot use its e-services. The dates are close, and the portal is the same. The audit concerns one group, but that is enough to contradict an unqualified claim.

Same portal, 2024: it caters to people with special needs, against persons with disabilities being unable to use e-services. Neither item records a change in accessibility between March and October 2024.

The Commission in October 2020 says the e-appeals section is being developed. North Macedonia says it was fully operational from 1 April 2019, covering the full appeals process. A later upgrade could reconcile them, but neither source says so. Low analytical weight.

Different points in the process. The tool can hold referral data while the referral itself is still issued on paper. The Commission's sentence is about paper use and interoperability, the country's about what the system stores. A tension remains, and practice needs checking.

As for the previous pair, but both statements are the Commission's. Storing referral data and issuing referrals on paper can both be true, particularly as the screening text describes content and not process. The later wording does not say paper was ended.

Same report and same time: the Central Register operates as the Point of Single Contact, against the Point of Single Contact being www.uslugi.gov.mk. The 2022 and 2024 reports also name the portal. The country may mean business registration only, but it does not limit its claim.

Fully aligned with the Directive against yet to align with it. The screening report was published four months after the 2024 report, and neither item records a change in the law in between. The Commission's 2023 report says the same as its 2024 report.

Same step and same 2025 assessment, confirmed from the section headings: the Law on Electronic Communications. The beneficiary says fully achieved, the Commission not achieved. This is an open disagreement on a payment-linked condition.
Same step, repeated after the December 2025 amendments: achieved against not achieved. This is the second such disagreement (see MKD-EU-2025-011) on a payment-linked condition.

Both late 2025. One says coverage is in line with the EU average (77% against 78%), the other below it (79.6% against 93.1%). The EU averages are too far apart to be the same measure, but neither text explains this. The strategy gives no year, and its diagnosis that price is the main challenge rests on the comparison.

Different measures and probably sources. ITU gives a survey-style share for 2020, and notes that its own table has 79.9% for all internet access. The Commission's undated 73.58% appears to be a regulator-style figure, and its next report gives 77.92% for 2021. Neither is defined.

'No data' most likely refers to the series the Commission used, not to the national statistics. The chart's years are also matched by position only, and the item is flagged for checking against the original PDF. Check before relying on this.
Same roaming regime, two start dates: 1 June and 1 July 2021. Other Commission reports also say July. Low analytical weight.

Phases of one agreement. Other Commission text (MKD-EU-2020-002, MKD-EU-2021-002) describes progressive reductions from July 2019 and elimination under roam like at home on 1 July 2021. The wording 'entered into force' in the second item is loose, but the sequence is compatible.

Same plan, about the same time, two end dates. No text describes a 2019-2023 phase of a 2019-2029 plan. The Commission says 2019-2023 in 2024 and 2019-2029 in 2025. Low analytical weight, except when the plan's expiry is being assessed.

Different scope. The Agency speaks of its own progress in applying the framework, under the heading of its recommendations. The Commission's rating covers the whole sub-area, including legislation and capacity. The Agency's next sentence goes on to list remaining actions.

As for the 2024 pair: the Agency's view of its own application of the framework against the Commission's rating of the whole sub-area. The Agency's own report relays the Commission's finding, which suggests it does not see the two as opposed.

Both 2025 and about the same legislation. The audit says flatly that national data protection legislation is aligned with EU legislation. The Commission says legislation to fully align with the GDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive is still pending, and calls the framework insufficient.

Formal status against degree of alignment. The Agency says the law transposes the GDPR. On the same page it relays the Commission's finding that full alignment is still to be completed. Its own strategy says further efforts are needed for full transposition.

As for the 2024 pair. The Agency states what the law transposes and, on the same page, relays that the framework is not fully aligned. The 'high level of protection' wording is an assertion of the law's purpose and does not deny the gap.

Opposite ratings of the same framework: robust, comprehensive and closely aligned against insufficient. Both are evaluative, and they are a year apart, with the NATO transfer amendment in between. The Agency's own strategy (page 13) concedes that full transposition is still to come.

Legal status against financial autonomy. The country describes the body's status under the law. The Commission says it is not fully autonomous financially. The word 'fully' and the narrow subject make the two compatible.

Legal status against operating independence. The Agency's statement is its description of status in the law. The Commission's concerns autonomy in hiring and budget. The Agency's report itself recommends securing independent functioning.

Legal status against budgetary independence. The Agency's own 2025 report (pages 5, 7, 9 and 32) says it lacks budgetary and human resources independence, so its statement of status is not a claim of practical autonomy.

Same law: fully aligned against further efforts needed. The law was not replaced until June 2025. In the screening report the Commission said it could not yet fully evaluate the claim, so the Commission's position is stated more firmly in the 2024 report.

Same Agency, same year, same action: reprimands in 10 cases against 4 cases. Other figures in the two sentences match (170 supervisions, 300 complaints, 15 opinions), so the count definition does not appear to differ.

Same Agency and year: reprimands in 17 cases against 4. Other figures match. The screening report gives 17 as the number of opinions in 2021, which may be relevant when the figures are checked against the Agency's own report.

Different registers and level. The country speaks of the National Real Estate Register in one central database. The Commission speaks of property registers, particularly at municipal level. The 2022 report also says land registration was completed. The extraction basis notes the same doubt.

Both from North Macedonia's authorities in 2025 about the same Directive: not aligned against partially aligned. Neither item records a change in the law. Mainly a difference of degree, with limited analytical weight.
Same law, two adoption dates: 2018 against February 2020. The run also holds the law's text as MKD-GOV-2020-001. Low analytical weight.

Different objects. The World Bank cites a global index ranking, which measures national commitments. The audit tests whether institutions protect critical systems in practice. A good index rank and poor practical protection can both be true.

Different editions and scales. The World Bank does not name the edition, and its footnote cites the index only. The 2024 item gives a tier, not a rank out of 182. 'Advanced' is the World Bank's own description and not an index category.

ITU lists the Law on Security of Network and Information Systems as an existing enabler in February 2022. The Commission says that the draft was not adopted in October 2022, and the law's text in the run is dated July 2025. ITU may have meant a draft, but it does not say so.

Same Council, two formation dates: July 2020 against 2019. A decision and an operational start could differ, but neither source says so. Low analytical weight, though the audit's findings on the Council's inactivity rest on the period since formation.

The footnote says the law aligns with NIS2, not that it fully aligns. The Commission concludes that it has sufficient alignment with NIS2 and that this element is achieved, while noting gaps. The two statements agree on the essentials.
Same action plan, two periods: 2025-2027 in its own title against 2025-2028 in the Commission's text. The Commission may be borrowing the strategy's period. Low analytical weight.
Same year and same origin, the MKD-CIRT figures: 1,443 against 1,441. No definition explains the two. Immaterial in size, but it may be worth noting that chart labels in the audit are converted text.

In context, 'this' refers to the steps on 5G expertise and the auction, not to all toolbox measures. The Commission's request to 'continue' implementation does not deny that much is done, and supplier risk assessment is not addressed by the Reform Agenda sentence.

Both Commission and no change in the law recorded between: yet to align with eIDAS in October 2022 against a legal environment harmonised with eIDAS since 2020, stated in 2023. The by-laws cited predate the first statement.
Both Commission, within four months in 2023: alignment with eIDAS further delayed against a legal environment already harmonised with eIDAS. No new law in between would explain this.

Same law and same year. The strategy says the 2019 law is aligned with European digitalisation legislation. The Commission says alignment with the regulation that law implements was further delayed. The strategy's wording is general, so this is a weaker case than the Commission's own conflict.

Commission reports a year apart: alignment further delayed against national law harmonised with the 2014 Regulation, with no amendment to the law in the list for that period (MKD-GOV-2025-009-0003). The 2024 report may be restating the position in the 2023 screening report.

The footnote claims alignment with the Regulation, not full alignment. The Commission says the law is not fully aligned but has reached sufficient alignment for the step, with a minimal deviation. The two statements agree on the essentials.

Same assessment: all preparatory activities completed against a self-assessment still to be finalised and a trusted list still to be published. The country's 'preparatory' could be narrower, but the Commission lists steps the country counts as done, such as applying the checklists.
Same step and same assessment, confirmed from the section headings: the trusted list. Achieved against not achieved, on a payment-linked condition.

The screening report says the framework is aligned with version 2.0 of the European framework, and its next sentence says it should be aligned with the latest version. The report only asks for alignment with the 2017 revision. The two statements describe the same position.

Different levels. Once-only is a rule about not asking citizens again, which can be applied without electronic exchange. The strategy speaks of electronic communication between public bodies generally. The two are in tension, but they do not strictly exclude each other.

Both from the country's government, about a year apart: once-only principle applied, against institutions still not gathering evidence ex officio as the law requires. Ex officio gathering is how once-only works in practice, and the 2024 text says the failure has lasted 9 years.

Different measures and periods. The Commission's 'use' has no metric and covers its reporting period to 2020. The audit measures traffic over 2019 to 2021, and attributes the high 2019 figure to frequent calls between particular institutions. Use could rise by some measures while traffic falls.

The country's own next sentence says storing documents as machine-readable or structured data is challenging. So both accept the same gap: technical readiness in general, but structured data still to do. The Commission's point is legal alignment.
